issues.item: Triggers: Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
issues.explanation: The trigger 'When people say things like my ex' is difficult to reconcile with a military trauma profile and the rest of the selected items, which center on combat/injury/hypervigilance cues. It introduces an interpersonal/romantic reminder theme that is otherwise unsupported by the memory, threat, appraisal, and strategy items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'I feel permanently humiliated by what happened' is not impossible after military trauma, but in this profile it sits somewhat apart from the rest of the formulation, which is dominated by injury cues, hypervigilance, fragmentation, outsider beliefs, and self-blame. The combination is not a direct contradiction on its own, but paired with the relationship-reminder trigger it suggests a mismatched interpersonal/shame theme that is insufficiently anchored elsewhere in the profile.

vignette:
Liam presents as a 28-year-old man struggling to reconcile his current life as a social media manager with his past as an infantryman. The trauma occurred nine months ago during his deployment in Afghanistan. His convoy was struck by an IED while navigating a narrow pass. Liam was in the lead vehicle, and the explosion threw him against the interior wall. He remembers the deafening roar, the acrid smell of smoke, and a chaotic sequence of images: the driver's grievous injuries, the frantic shouts over the radio, the rhythmic whump-whump of the incoming medevac helicopter. To keep these images from ambushing him at night, he has started forcing himself to stay awake until he collapses from exhaustion, the only state in which his mind feels quiet. He reports that the memory itself feels fundamentally broken; it exists not as a story but as a collection of sensory shards that refuse to cohere, making it hard to believe it even happened to him. When a fragment does break through, the thought that follows is always the same: that his mind is shattered beyond repair, confirming his deepest fear that he is permanently broken. In the aftermath of these intrusions, he finds himself on high alert, his focus narrowing to seek out anything that might signal a similar loss of control, a desperate attempt to preempt the next ambush from his own mind.

In the months since his return, these fragments have become landmines in his daily life. Because the memory of the chaotic aftermath is so potent, he now finds himself scanning his environment for any sign of disorder or injury, making him hyper-alert to things he previously would not have noticed. The sound of a distant helicopter, a common occurrence in his city, is no longer benign. The moment he hears the blades, he is no longer in his apartment but back in the pass, the rhythmic whump-whump of the medevac chopper filling the air as he tastes dust and smoke. It immediately triggers a cascade of physical reactions-his heart pounds, his palms sweat, and a wave of pure, imageless terror washes over him, the same raw emotion he felt in the vehicle but without a clear picture to attach it to. This profound sense of threat has bled into every corner of his existence. He finds it nearly impossible to fall asleep, convinced he must remain alert for some unspecified danger, and his partner has learned not to touch him unexpectedly, as his startled reactions have become increasingly volatile. The constant feeling of being on edge means he is perpetually scanning his environment, which only makes him more likely to encounter things that send him back to that moment.

These triggers and the intense threat they provoke have reshaped his world into a landscape of things to be avoided. After seeing a cyclist with a scraped and bloody leg on his commute, the raw sight of the injury sent him into a tailspin, reinforcing his belief that he is permanently damaged. In response, he has begun to avoid any situation that puts his body under stress, quitting his gym and turning down invitations to play basketball with friends. Driving, especially with other people in the car, feels impossibly dangerous, a direct echo of the helplessness he felt in the convoy. This has led to him making excuses to work from home, jeopardizing his position at the marketing agency. The routes he no longer drives and the friends he no longer sees have become their own silent reminders of the trauma, a map of avoidance that constantly reinforces what he has lost. Each act of avoidance serves as confirmation of his own brokenness; rehearsing what he needs to say before a simple phone call reinforces the painful belief that he is now an outsider, incapable of normal human interaction.

This cycle of memory, threat, and avoidance has become a tightly sealed loop. A fragmented memory-the scent of hot metal, the feeling of being thrown-will surge up, prompting a powerful sense of imminent danger. This feeling of threat then compels him to retreat further, cancelling plans or refusing to leave his apartment. This avoidance, in turn, prevents any new learning from taking place; it stops him from ever discovering that a car ride can be safe or that physical exertion is just exercise. Without any disconfirming evidence, his body has no reason to stop sounding the alarm; the feeling of imminent threat therefore remains at a constant, exhausting high. By retreating, his nervous system has only learned one lesson: that avoidance works, which has cemented the belief that the world is unmanageably dangerous and that he is right to feel terrified. By shrinking his world, he ensures the traumatic memory remains unprocessed, its fragments sharp and potent. The very strategies he uses to feel safe only amplify his conviction that he has been permanently changed for the worse, a belief that primes him to interpret even ambiguous stimuli as threats. Seeing a police officer in uniform is no longer a neutral event; it is a visceral reminder of a world of violence he can't escape, confirming his identity as someone who will never truly belong to civilian life again. He came to therapy after his partner found him sitting in the dark, hours after a car backfired outside, saying he was "done." He expressed a desperate fear that he is losing himself completely and a fragile hope that he might one day feel safe in his own skin.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not describe a causal link where the trauma memory itself directly leads to maladaptive strategies.
The vignette does not describe a causal link where the trauma memory itself directly leads to negative appraisals.
The vignette does not describe a causal link where the trauma memory makes the patient more sensitive or hypervigilant to triggers.
The vignette does not describe a causal link where maladaptive strategies make the patient more likely to encounter triggers.
The vignette does not describe a causal link where maladaptive strategies heighten the patient's overall sense of threat.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not describe a causal link where the trauma memory itself directly leads to maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not describe a causal link where the trauma memory itself directly leads to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not describe a causal link where the trauma memory makes the patient more sensitive or hypervigilant to triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not describe a causal link where maladaptive strategies make the patient more likely to encounter triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not describe a causal link where maladaptive strategies heighten the patient's overall sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
